title: Marine boundary layer influence on satellite AOD and surface PM 2.5  during coastal California wildfires
content: Wildfire smoke is a major driver of fine particulate matter concentrations (PM2.5; particles ≤2.5 µm in diameter) in coastal California, yet satellite aerosol optical depth (AOD) can deviate from surface concentrations when the marine boundary-layer (MBL) structure is present, potentially biasing real-time estimates of communities at risk of exposure. We compared two contrasting Southern California wildfire periods: the Mountain fire (November 2024; Santa Ana winds) and the Gifford fire (August 2025; onshore MBL). Daily domain-mean MODIS Aqua AOD (550 nm) was paired with surface PM2.5 from U.S. EPA regulatory monitors and PurpleAir (PA) sensors to quantify column-surface coupling, evaluate distance-dependent impacts, and test predictive utility using ridge regression. During the 21-day plume window, the Mountain fire showed significant AOD-PM2.5 coupling (Spearman ρ = 0.565, p = 0.012; n = 19; combined EPA and PA), consistent with reduced marine-layer shielding under offshore flow. In contrast, the Gifford fire demonstrated a decoupling of column-surface concentrations (ρ = 0.346, p = 0.135; n = 20) despite higher mean AOD (0.1317 vs. 0.0440), consistent with MBL serving as a structural barrier to plume surface penetration. Distance-stratified results (15–66 km) varied in magnitude but preserved this overall pattern; designated backside PA sites, analyzed separately, captured elevated concentrations. AOD-only ridge models performed worse than the mean baseline for both fires. Adding meteorology and smoke indicators improved performance: best gains of +0.27 (Mountain fire; AOD + HMS) and +0.59 (Gifford fire; AOD + ERA5). Overall, coastal AOD-PM2.5 coupling depends on boundary-layer structure and transport, supporting integrated use of satellite AOD, meteorology, and denser surface monitoring in sparsely sampled coastal and mountainous regions.
